title: [FIXTURE] Job Role: Data Analyst
text:

A data analyst collects, cleans, and interprets data sets to answer questions and support decisions. Typical responsibilities include preparing data for analysis, building dashboards and reports, and communicating findings to stakeholders.

Commonly required skills for a data analyst include SQL for querying databases, a spreadsheet tool such as Excel, a data visualisation tool, and increasingly a scripting language such as Python or R. Statistical literacy and clear communication are core to the role.

Adjacent roles include business analyst, data engineer, and data scientist. A data analyst who deepens statistical modelling and machine learning skills may progress toward data scientist roles, while one who deepens pipeline and infrastructure skills may progress toward data engineering.

title: [FIXTURE] Job Role: Software Developer
text:

A software developer designs, builds, tests, and maintains software applications. Day-to-day work typically involves writing and reviewing code, debugging, collaborating with designers and product managers, and deploying software.

Common skills include proficiency in one or more programming languages such as Python, Java, or JavaScript, version control with Git, testing practices, and familiarity with cloud platforms. Problem decomposition and teamwork are essential soft skills.

Career progression commonly moves from junior developer to senior developer, then branches into technical leadership (staff engineer, architect) or people management (engineering manager).

title: [FIXTURE] Job Role: Cybersecurity Analyst
text:
FIXTURE SAMPLE — placeholder content for development.

A cybersecurity analyst monitors systems for security incidents, investigates alerts, and helps an organisation protect its information assets. Responsibilities include monitoring security tooling, triaging and responding to incidents, performing vulnerability assessments, and supporting security awareness.

Common skills include networking fundamentals, operating system administration, security monitoring tools, incident response procedures, and scripting for automation. Foundational knowledge areas include threat landscapes, access control, and security frameworks.

Adjacent roles include security engineer, penetration tester, and governance-risk-compliance specialist.

title: [FIXTURE] Skill: SQL
text:

SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for querying and manipulating relational databases. It is a foundational skill for data analysts, data engineers, business intelligence developers, and many software developer roles.

Proficiency levels typically progress from writing basic SELECT queries with filtering and joins, to aggregations and window functions, to query optimisation and schema design. SQL is frequently combined with spreadsheet tools, visualisation tools, and Python in analytics workflows.

title: [FIXTURE] Skill: Python Programming
text:

Python is a general-purpose programming language widely used in data analysis, machine learning, automation, and web development. For analytics roles, commonly used Python libraries include pandas for data manipulation and matplotlib or similar libraries for visualisation.

Python is relevant to data analysts, data scientists, software developers, and increasingly to non-technical roles that automate repetitive work. It pairs naturally with SQL and data visualisation skills.

title: [FIXTURE] Skill: Data Visualisation
text:

Data visualisation is the practice of representing data graphically so that patterns and insights are easy to understand. It covers choosing appropriate chart types, designing dashboards, and communicating findings to non-technical audiences.

It is a core skill for data analysts and business analysts and complements SQL and Python. Common tooling categories include business intelligence dashboard tools and charting libraries.

An introductory data analytics course typically covers: working with spreadsheets, basic SQL queries, introductory statistics, and building simple dashboards. Such courses are commonly aimed at career switchers and professionals who want to add data skills to their current role.

Typical prerequisites are basic computer literacy; no prior programming experience is usually assumed at the introductory level.

title: [FIXTURE] Career Pathway: Switching into Data Analytics
text:
FIXTURE SAMPLE — placeholder content for development.

A common pathway into data analytics from a non-technical role (for example marketing or operations) starts by applying data skills inside the current job: analysing campaign or operations data with spreadsheets, then learning SQL, then a visualisation tool, then Python.

Career switchers typically build a small portfolio of analysis projects using public data sets, which demonstrates practical skills to employers. Transferable strengths from prior roles — domain knowledge, stakeholder communication, and project delivery — are valued in analyst positions.

title: [FIXTURE] Insight: Why Skills-Based Hiring Is Growing
text:
FIXTURE SAMPLE — placeholder content for development.

Employers increasingly describe vacancies in terms of skills rather than qualifications alone. For job seekers, this means that demonstrable skills — evidenced by portfolios, certifications, and work samples — can matter as much as formal credentials.

For planning a career move, a practical approach is: identify the target role, list the skills it commonly requires, map them against your current skills, and close the highest-priority gaps through training or on-the-job projects.
